claims.text: The coating's creep resistance is primarily controlled by a high density of FCC/BCC phase boundaries.
FCC/BCC interfaces impede dislocation slip and climb during sustained loading.
Dynamic recovery at FCC/BCC boundaries produces stabilized subgrain structures during creep.
Boundary-associated stabilized subgrains slow progressive plastic deformation.
Mechanically alloyed, nanocrystalline CoCrFeNiTi-type HEAs can exhibit a dual FCC/BCC microstructure.
The relevant protective coating has well-distributed FCC/BCC interphase boundaries.
A controlled heat treatment can change the FCC/BCC phase fractions without changing overall composition.
Increasing the BCC phase fraction will increase the density of FCC/BCC phase boundaries.
The BCC phase is harder, intrinsically stronger, and less diffusive than the FCC phase.
The BCC phase acts as a barrier to dislocations originating in the more ductile FCC phase.
Dislocations accumulate at FCC/BCC interfaces under sustained high-temperature stress.
Dynamic recovery of accumulated dislocations promotes subgrain formation at the interfaces.
The resulting subgrains further hinder dislocation climb and slip and thereby reduce creep strain rate.
At identical test conditions, a coating with greater BCC phase fraction and phase-boundary density will have a lower creep strain rate than the baseline coating.
At identical test conditions, a coating with greater BCC phase fraction and phase-boundary density will accumulate less total creep strain than the baseline coating.
The mechanism applies near 0.8 Tm when creep is governed by diffusion and dislocation motion.
The mechanism is not expected to govern when oxidation, phase transformations, or other degradation mechanisms prevail.
Analogous prior studies support a qualitative role for phase boundaries in impeding dislocation motion.
A cited FCC high-entropy superalloy with L12 precipitates had a creep-rupture life of approximately 114 hours at 982 degrees Celsius and 159 MPa.
